speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, I will speak on delivering healthcare to our fellow Singaporeans and supporting our sisters and brothers working on the healthcare frontline.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak on five areas today: (a) seniors' access to care; (b) care coordination; (c) care-givers; (d) IT and design in healthcare; and (e) our healthcare frontliners.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In an ageing society, we have more Singaporeans with mobility needs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has MOH studied whether seniors in such households are more likely to miss medical appointments?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has MOH looked at how to better support such seniors so they can more easily get to the clinic so that chronic diseases can be brought under control better and so that hospital admissions can be reduced by going upstream?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH look into better support for home delivery of medications?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because this too will reduce the need for seniors with limited mobility to make multiple outpatient trips.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On my Clementi home visits, I have met residents who have many, many medical appointments.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Each of them will mean her daughter has to take time off from work to accompany her to and from the clinic for the appointment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: With an ageing population and shrinking family sizes, this poses a challenge for many seniors in the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In some cases, the son or daughter cannot take leave or has used up all of their annual leave, or the family member may be a low-wage worker, daily-rated, which means time away from work becomes loss of income.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many patients today are older, with more medical conditions—more complex medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes three, four, five – even more – medical teams look after the same patient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can look at reimagining our healthcare so as to support this better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are lessons we can learn for coordinating care across other medical conditions as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some years ago, as a young doctor, I looked after an old lady with advanced cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She was very, very sick and not getting better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He quit his job to look after his mother.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He found it so hard getting back into the workforce in his fifties.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet this man, this filial caring son, had shown dedication and devotion to duty, day and night, looking after his mother who was terminally ill.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Dedication, devotion, duty, but unfortunately, potential employers did not see it that way.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They asked, "What is this gap in your CV?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Why were you out of the workforce?" They did not see the dedication and devotion to duty.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Together, across the Ministries, together with industry, and with our brothers and sisters in the Unions, we can find ways to build awareness among employers and even go the extra mile to recognise inclusive employers, who hire fellow Singaporeans who are returning to the workforce having spent time as care-givers showing that dedication and devotion to duty.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chairman, when we empower our healthcare workers, when we look at what is happening on the ground and empower workers on the ground to do their jobs better, it helps patients as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is it faster, easier, than ticking boxes and signing a piece of paper?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If it is not, we must ask ourselves why and how can it be improved?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do they speed things up, so healthcare workers can spend more time, more quality time with patients?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And if so, why and how can we make it better?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Computer workstations today, the design of workstations today, computers, do they help doctors and nurses maintain eye contact with the patient?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Comfort the patients, especially in a world with COVID-19, where everyone is wearing a mask and that eye contact becomes even more important.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How much time it takes to get a task done?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How much movement is needed to make something happen?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has there been any recent ergonomic research to see what brings more comfort to patients and better performance for healthcare workers?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But what we do not study, what we no not look at, what we do not search for, we do not know.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every iPhone user everyone who uses a modern multi-touch smartphone, sees the impact of his influence and legacy on industrial design.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: His younger sister Mona wrote in the New York Times shortly after he passed away.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She wrote about how Steve Jobs, from his hospital bed, as a patient battling terminal cancer, wanted to make the hospital better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sketching devices to hold an iPad in a hospital bed, designing new fluid monitors and X-ray equipment, re-drawing the design of a hospital unit.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not every one of us can be Steve Jobs, but every patient brings an important perspective to the healthcare journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And when we see better through the eyes of our patients, when we see better through the eyes of our healthcare workers on the ground, we continually see better and better ways to improve our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can apply the same care and attention and passion to re-imagining the design of healthcare facilities, re-imagining the user experience so healthcare workers can do the job even better, care for patients even better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Whether it is a hospital computer system, the healthcare workplace, or the patient journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In particular, I want to salute our nurses and allied health workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every doctor knows this instinctively, even before they become a doctor from their days as a medical student.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The impact our nurses have, lifting up the lives of our patients making a difference for every patient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I say this both as a doctor and as the son of a patient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see the impact that our nurses have, that care, that dedication, that heart.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Nursing is also deeply skilled work, deeply skilled work and essential work.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some years ago, I attended a healthcare conference.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One of the speaker was the President and CEO of the Duke University Hospital in the USA.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He is a nurse, trained as an Oncology nurse, rose up through the ranks to lead the hospital, to lead an entire healthcare system in the USA.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should continue looking at ways to further empower our nurses in Singapore to create more opportunities for upskilling and advancement, as we all work together to lift up the lives of our patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These are some of our outsourced healthcare frontline workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our hospital cleaners, our healthcare attendants are an integral part of the health care workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Facing the COVID-19 risks together, serving on the same front line as medical nursing and allied health staff serving together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Once upon a time all these brothers and sisters were directly hired by the hospitals and not outsourced.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: First of all, the demand for hospital cleaners and hospital attendants is the same throughout the year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It does not vary much throughout the year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And in a COVID-19 world, it makes sense for team members to stay based within the same healthcare institution rather than moving from place to place amidst a pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We are already providing outsourced cleaners with protective gear during COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It recognises that they are part of the same healthcare frontline.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And there is something to be said for treating all our hospital cleaners and healthcare attendants as part of the in-house staff, making them feel more fully like part of the team, supporting resourcing, uplifting these workers together accordingly.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In my Meet-the-People Sessions in Clementi, I have met older workers who have been retrenched, who are looking for job placements in healthcare institutions nearby.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chairman, healthcare is about "health" and "care" supporting our patients, supporting our care-givers, supporting our healthcare workers –our sisters and brothers on the healthcare frontline.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is about keeping all of us safe, keeping all of us safe together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, may we continue building a healthier Singapore as we fight this COVID-19 pandemic as we emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, achieving herd immunity through COVID-19 vaccinations is important to our economy and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even with the commencement of the vaccination programme for senior citizens, some of my senior residents shared that they are adopting the wait-and-see approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I cite some of the most common reasons pertaining to their decision.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, the two approved vaccines in Singapore are based on a novel technology, so the long-term effects are unknown.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some are also questioning the need for vaccination as the community infection rates are low.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may not go for the vaccination if there is no need for a vaccination certificate to travel.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is outreach also extended to younger Singaporeans pertaining to elderly vaccinations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some elderly said that their children or grandchildren discouraged them from taking it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is because their children are worried that the vaccinations have dangerous implications on seniors with health complications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does MOH plan to encourage more seniors in the community to get vaccinated?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID) was officially opened in September 2019, just a few months before Singapore detected the first confirmed case of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thereafter, NCID played a crucial role in battling COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On the whole, Singapore has done relatively well in controlling the number of community cases as compared to our neighbouring countries, Asia and the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Certainly, we are not perfect and can do better with the benefit of hindsight.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, we could have advised Singaporeans to wear reusable masks earlier.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Also, the outbreak of COVID-19 at the foreign worker's dormitories caught us by surprise.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We could have moved in earlier to improve their living conditions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Having said that, COVID-19 will not be our last pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We need to document the main learning points of managing COVID-19 and learn from it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This would be similar to what the MOF did by releasing the "Interim Assessment of the Impact of Key COVID-19 Budget Measures".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We know that the pandemic is not over yet, but an interim report will be important as what has transpired in the past year is still fresh in our memory.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: More importantly, we would like to know how MOH and Singapore could be better prepared for the next disease X.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has put a strain on healthcare services and facilities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: First, COVID-19 has delayed the construction of healthcare facilities in Singapore, but the growth in our ageing population is marching on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Second, I am concern about the difficulty in employing domestic helpers to care for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many Nanyang residents have approached me to appeal for elder care or nursing home facilities, because of the challenges in bringing in domestic helpers to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How can the MOH cope with this sudden surge in demand, especially with the delay in the construction of nursing homes?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Besides the need for nursing homes for elderly that are not able to take care of themselves, there is also a strong interest from the more abled elderly to age in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Research shows poverty often overwhelms one's cognitive ability to make good decisions on health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I, thus, speak on the urgent need to tackle health inequality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would seem that the prevalence of conditions like obesity, diabetes, hypertension and high cholesterol has risen over the years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While many efforts have been undertaken, the outcome seems to be moving in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To achieve better outcomes, we need better measurement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Other than the response to my recent Parliamentary Question for what I understand the most recent publicly available data on health risks, behaviours and outcomes by socio-economic class was 2010 National Health Survey.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The National Registry of Diseases already collects data on the incidence of cancer and chronic kidney failure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is an easy next step to include SES indicators like income and education.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must also study the entire life cycle of chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are low-income groups contracting more diseases, more severe diseases or even earlier diseases?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are they receiving a later diagnosis with poorer outcomes compared to wealthy Singaporeans who can choose top tier private care, for example?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not suggesting that this is the case but it would be useful to have the data.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some doctors have observed COVID-19-related backlogs and patients transferring from private to public to save money, pressuring the public system and lengthening waiting times for subsidised patients.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, could we develop a National Health Equity Index?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This could be created by an independent group of academics and include social determinants of health as well as health care accessibility, affordability and outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How effective have the incentives been among lower income groups?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Other than the number of participants, can we targets in terms of better health outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The National Health Screening Programme, Screen for Life, heavily subsidies screening for some conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What is the take-up rate and outcomes thus far, particularly for those who are less advantaged socio-economically?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, we must improve outcomes at the intersection of health inequality and preventive health care.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Not only because we have a responsibility to the less fortunate but also because this problem creates spill-over effects that can cause society more if left untreated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, escalating healthcare cost is a major worry for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since cost is a result of the prices set by the public healthcare institutions, the pricing principles of the public sector is of great interest to us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is public health pricing based on average cost or marginal cost?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the various cost components incorporated in those costs?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the cost-based price checked against the pricing of other countries?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the other considerations in determining the final price?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how does MOH monitor and change the pricing overtime?

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, it is not uncommon for us to hear senior residents complaining about 可以病，不可以死。可以死，不可以病。Which means that can fall ill but cannot die.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But with rapid medical technological and pharmaceutical advances, costs of healthcare delivery have increased exponentially.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But this appears to be a global situation.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The average global medical inflation rate was observed at 9.7% that year.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As the population ages, more spending on healthcare will be required and the rate of medical inflation will need to be checked.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How is MOH keeping track of the medical inflation trend and looking into its impact on Singaporeans?

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The average Singaporean household expenses on healthcare costs in 2017 and 2018 were found to have increased by 4.5 to 5.5 percentage point as from five years ago.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How much does the average Singaporean household spend on healthcare?

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And how does it compare to other developed countries?

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are our current MediSave contributions keeping pace with the medical inflation?

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our "3M" framework public financing healthcare plays a crucial role to keep quality of health care affordable for all.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has announced that there will higher remuneration for our nurses and healthcare support staff, which I fully concur with.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, we must now also examine how to fund the inevitable increases in healthcare expenses.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With our ageing population, our elderly will be saddled with more healthcare costs pertaining to illness.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last year, I voiced my concerns for senior citizens who had to pay upfront cash for age-related medical treatments.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Naturally, we must ensure MediSave contributions would commensurate with the higher medical expenses.

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: When is our last review of our MediSave contributions?

speaker: Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Will the Ministry do a review on our current "3M" health financing strategy to ensure all Singaporeans will be adequately covered and keep up with medical inflation?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, MediSave limits are a major concern for the elderly and it is the issue I have been asked most frequently to raise.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In November last year, Senior Minister of State said that MediSave limits are being reviewed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on the status of the review?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the moment, MediSave can be used mainly for hospitalisation and in-patient treatment with limited outpatient treatments allowed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Limiting MediSave to mainly in-patient treatment skews demand towards hospitalisation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Outpatient treatment is cheaper and can manage disease before they worsen and become more costly to treat.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we can allow MediSave to be used more widely on out-patient treatments, we can shift demand towards the lower cost outpatient treatments and help control healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister consider expanding the range of outpatient treatments allowed to use MediSave?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many seniors suffer from chronic conditions which require extended care and that can be very expensive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most outpatient treatment is not covered by MediShield Life and access to MediFund is only available to the very low income.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The use of MediSave is subject to annual withdrawal caps.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can have an undesirable effect of discouraging seniors from seeking early treatment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can be rolled out at polyclinics, restructured hospitals and CHAS clinics where tight procedures are already in place to ensure that only medically necessary treatment is prescribed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the Government has responded decisively in deploying resources to combat the COVID-19 pandemic with healthcare expenditures increased significantly to provide for our public health management measures.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, even without the pandemic, we know that the healthcare expenditure has been rising globally.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Globally, we are also seeing similar trends in developed countries due to increasing medical attention, medication, procedures and longer hospital stays from an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, the Government has been working on making our health care accessible and affordable through investing in medical infrastructure, establishing "P" benchmarks, providing various subsidies, as well as working with Singaporeans to encourage a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has worked well for Singaporeans thus far.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we cannot ignore the rising healthcare costs that Singaporeans may face.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we continue to provide higher value in healthcare in the face of rising healthcare costs and ageing population and advances in medical procedures?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Value in healthcare is generated by delivering better health outcomes for the same or a lower cost.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While our healthcare costs have been rising each year, we currently do not have a very clear grasp if healthcare outcomes of major or common diseases, such as diabetes or asthma have been improving.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Healthcare providers have typically been paid on a fee-for-service model with subvention given mainly by volume.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The objective of health, value-based healthcare, is to create financial incentive to encourage providers to improve the health value given to patients.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One example is from Sweden's National Health System where they piloted a bundled payment model for cataract and hip replacement procedure.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The bundle sets a single base price that covers the entire care delivery chain from diagnostic surgery to follow-up visits.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Providers are paid based on whether they met pre-defined health outcomes to the patient.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This has helped in the pilot years for complications to decrease by 18% re-operations to fall by 23%.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I acknowledge that there are no silver bullets to address the rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will consider value-based healthcare incentive approach as an important part of the short and long-term strategy to achieve better healthcare value for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: More transparency on the data and assumptions used will help to better to explain these premium hikes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Last November, in response to my request for the release of the full MediShield Life actuarial report, Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon, said that MOH may engage different consultants to challenge the assumptions and do another calculation and publish some of this data in an academic way.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Will the full MediShield Life actuarial report be provided to these consultants and academics for further analysis?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And if so, when will this be done?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Lastly, I note that the new MediShield Life premiums have kicked in on 1 of March.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Mr Chairman, the issue of portable health insurance was raised by Health Correspondent Salma Khalik in December last year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As a person gets older, it becomes difficult to move from one insurer to another.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: This is because people develop medical problems as they grow older.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: When they tried to switch insurers, they generally face the prospect of these pre-existing conditions being excluded from cover.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: As a result, beyond a certain age, it becomes practically impossible for people to switch to another insurer even if there is a big difference in premiums paid.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I need to first declare conflict of interest as a general surgeon in private practice, with an interest in breast surgery; and my role as the elected President of Singapore Medical Association.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Escalating healthcare costs is a concern for many governments.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, this has gained much attention recently with questions raised by the public on private insurance agents.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In truth, managing healthcare costs is a complex problem.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Learned economists have studied it, and there is no simple answer.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As research and experimental trials become validated, the advances will be accepted in mainstream clinical practice.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: One simple example in my field – 30 years ago, most breast cancer patients had to accept a mastectomy, and the resulting change in appearance was unacceptable to some.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Now, patients can opt for nipple-sparing mastectomy and immediate reconstruction which allow the patient to regain a physical appearance which is similar to her normal.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This means a better outcome for some patients, but clearly, increase costs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Who monitors the costs of the private healthcare facilities?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As a patient, when I receive the itemised bill, how do I know which of these items are reasonably charged, and which are not?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Doctors' fees have often been blamed as the main source of increased costs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Since then, the benchmarks serve as a guide on how doctors charge.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: When people fall sick, how do they choose their care?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Do they go to a polyclinic, the emergency department or straight to a specialist?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Patients factor in financial costs when they need to see a doctor.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some will go only to their company doctors based on their corporate insurances with no need to pay out of pocket.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: When they need to have hospital admissions, day surgery or major operations, that is when their Integrated Shield Plans will come in useful.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In my Budget debate speech, I highlighted the importance of shared decision making in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We are in the age of patient empowerment.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This has been so for quite a few years with an increasingly better educated population.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The Judiciary has acknowledged this trend when they introduced the Modified Montgomery Test and the understanding was reinforced by this Government when the Civil Law Act was amended last year.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Patients must be adequately informed before they make a choice on the medical care that they want to receive.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am all for this and medical practitioners here have been making adjustments in the way they practise, in order that patients are better informed and empowered.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, insurers need to share more information and allow their clients to make informed decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: From time to time, I get asked by friends and relatives about health insurance, especially Integrated Shield Plans or IPs in short.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: These questions include – which IP provider is better, and which IP plan provided by the provider is more suited to my needs?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I must admit I am ill-equipped to answer these questions.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I myself am insured with an IP, but I must confess that when I bought it many years ago, I did not make a detailed comparison of the various IP providers' offerings, but trusted my financial advisor's recommendation.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: So, IPs affect the majority of us living here.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore important that Singaporeans are adequately informed upfront by the various IP insurers before they make a decision to buy an IP, or before they make a decision to switch IP providers, since IPs are bought annually.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I ask myself, what would I like to know before I made a decision to buy a certain IP or not.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: These are the most important questions that will make me choose one IP provider over another.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: One, what are the premiums for me now and when I get older?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Two, what are the benefits and claim limits of each plan offered?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Three, what percentage of private sector specialists are empanelled by a certain IP provider?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Four, does the IP provider allow me to go to any private hospital in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Five, are all restructured hospital specialists automatically empanelled?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Questions about empanelling are important because ultimately, it is about choice.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The IP provider that offers more choices is more attractive to a potential IP customer.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The last question about how IP insurers pay specialists is important in an indirect way.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: A system that reimburses private sector specialists adequately is more sustainable and better for me as a policyholder, in the long run.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: More specialists will want to be empanelled with this IP provider and I will have a wider choice.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: If my IP insurer does not pay the specialist fairly or adequately, how would the doctor feel?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We can use the MOH fee benchmarks as a good guide for this.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: How does each IP provider pay specialists for procedures?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Does a certain IP insurer pay up to the higher limit of the benchmarks, or the lower limit, or up to the mid-point?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Or does this IP insurer reimburse at rates that are even lower than the lower limit of MOH fee benchmarks?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It should be a warning sign to policyholders when an IP provider pays doctors below or only at the lower limit of the MOH benchmarks.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I think the regulators of IPs, which are MAS and MOH, can obtain the answers to these six questions from IP insurers and present them in a tabulated and easily digestible form that members of the public can refer to when they make their decisions on which IP to buy.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This will advance the cause of patient education and empowerment.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: A more difficult but important policy question to ask is what proportion of Singapore Residents should buy IP.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This is an unusual phenomenon in the running of a health insurance system.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In the normal scheme of things, healthy insurance policyholders subsidise policyholders who fall sick and make claims.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But in our IP environment, the business of IP is cross-subsidised not just by those who do not fall sick, but by those who fall sick and yet choose to be treated at subsidised B2 and C classes in restructured hospitals when they are entitled to more under their IPs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: At the superficial level, it would appear that there is nothing wrong with this because it is the patient's choice and it is good to be prudent.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is an externality cost, when IP holders choose subsidised wards in the restructured hospitals when they fall sick.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: These Government subsidies would not have been consumed had the patients chose what they were entitled to, to be treated in the private hospitals or in A or B1 class wards.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is important that we study this "voluntary downgrading" phenomenon so that we can ensure that the IP environment today is functioning faithfully to the original policy intent of IPs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Also, what is the desired proportion of Singapore residents who should buy IPs.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know the correct figure, but with a private sector market share of only 30% to 35%, including B1 and A class beds in restructured hospitals, the corresponding figure of 70% of the population having IPs sounds rather high.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Can the private sector support the needs of this 70% if all of them who fell ill chose the unsubsidised services they are entitled to under their IPs?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have a few patients who themselves are insurance agents, and they realise they do not quite know what they are covered for.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Are all insurance agents well trained and up-to-date about the products they are selling?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Are the medical underwriters also keeping their medical knowledge up to date?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I raise one specific and very common example in my field: a healthy lady in her 20s with no family history is offered a free health screening when she signs up for an IP, including ultrasound of the breasts.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This picks up a 3-mm nodule, too small to categorise.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This lady is then informed that she will be excluded from breast cancer coverage.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Thereafter, there is a cycle of her agent asking her to see a doctor, the doctor telling her it is likely benign and can observe.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The agent may then ask for a memo to state that she does not have cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I have met patients where they state that the agent has asked them to pay for the surgery themselves to remove the lump, and then appeal to be covered.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As a breast surgeon, I do not know how to help this group of affected women.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: There are no good medical indications for any of these.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Who is scrutinising the other players in the healthcare costs equation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can conduct a review and consider increasing the limits on the use of MediSave for IVF and not just on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be a pity for couples who are unable to afford it but have funds in their MediSave, to be denied the gift of parenthood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the dialogues I have organised on IVF, many couples told me that they have achieved better results from supplementing their IVF treatments with TCM.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some doctors recommend TCM treatment for certain patients as it may optimise results.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: TCM treatments such as acupuncture can act as a supplementary method for patients to increase their chances of success.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My wife also, upon the advice of our doctor, did TCM during our IVF treatments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some might say that TCM does not work, while others say it does, but we can all agree that it does help provide an ease of mind, that we have tried everything we can do to have a successful IVF cycle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we allow couples to use their MediSave which they are allowed to use for IVF and subject to the current withdrawal limits, for TCM treatments associated with IVF?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last month, I proposed extending co-funding to the seventh and eighth IVF cycles to support couples who need more cycles to conceive successfully.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOH responded that, "We also need to balance the need to meaningfully and responsibly allocate public funds on this." In this case, rather than provide additional funding after the sixth cycle, will MOH allow co-funding leftover from the first six subsidised IVF cycles to be rolled over into the seventh and eighth cycle?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can it also allow any co-funding leftover from the three subsidised fresh cycles to be used for the subsidised frozen cycles?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are funds the Government has already budgeted for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is win-win solution as it allows couples to complete additional cycles using subsidies that we have already budgeted for without additional allocation needed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Chairman, as we dedicate 2021 as the year of celebrating SG women and as a mother myself, I would like to dedicate this cut to bring attention to the health of pregnant women and how it can affect our children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Both overseas and local research have pointed to the impact of maternal health on the health of our children.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: One of such findings is from a homegrown Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes or GUSTO study conducted by researchers in the National University Health System, KK Women's and Children's Hospital and A*STAR Singapore Institute for Clinical Sciences over the last 10 years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Another concern pointed out by the study is the mental health of pregnant women.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: We know that causes for these diseases can be multi-faceted and complex, including the pregnant mothers' own health and her social economic environment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Pregnant mothers and disadvantaged circumstances are at even higher risk.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Lastly, how can the Government enable evidence-based information to be disseminated more effectively to more pregnant women to increase awareness and encourage self-care for the well-being of their children?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.01 pm until 3.25 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank Members for their speeches and their remarks.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Globally, the number of new cases and deaths continue to trend down, although there was a spike in the last week of February.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Within Singapore, the COVID-19 situation has stabilised, with one or two new community cases on some days.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Imported cases are isolated on arrival and the risk of transmission to the community is low.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, the World Health Organization has just warned that we need to stay vigilant as the pandemic is not likely to be over within this year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I want to thank everyone – Singaporeans, healthcare workers, businessmen, businesses, enterprises, Government agencies – for playing your part this past year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Your sacrifices have helped Singapore weather this storm.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the impact of COVID-19 on our infrastructure projects.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As I have informed the House earlier, the pandemic has delayed many of our healthcare infrastructure projects by up to a year or so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Construction works have since been ramping up progressively and we are working on contingency measures to ensure we are able to meet the needs of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are making steady progress in our vaccination programme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to say a few words in Mandarin please.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (In Mandarin):    Seniors are most at risk of severe outcomes if they are infected with COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, we have prioritised seniors in our vaccination programme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The vaccines approved for use in Singapore must meet stringent safety and efficacy standards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some Singaporeans with chronic diseases are worried about being vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Do not worry, because we will arrange for healthcare professionals on site to assess if you can be vaccinated safely.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In fact, most people can be vaccinated safely, including those with diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, asthma, chronic lung disease, heart disease and cancer patients in remission.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Hence, I encourage Singaporeans with these conditions to register for vaccination as soon as they are invited.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (In English): Let me emphasise that only COVID-19 vaccines that meet strict standards of safety and effectiveness will be used in Singapore for our Singapore Residents.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will monitor the development of the COVID-19 pandemic and adjust our measures accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also continue to strengthen our defences for future health system crises, such as Disease X.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will share more.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even as we mobilise the nation to fight COVID-19, we have to remain focused on long-term issues.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Members may recall our Three Beyonds to meet our challenges in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Beyond Hospital to Community, to provide better care closer to home; Beyond Quality to Value, to help Singaporeans stretch their dollar; and Beyond Healthcare to Health, to help Singaporeans stay healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) has been expanded recently to allow more Singaporeans to receive subsidised care from private GPs, who are our key partners in primary care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will add new Community Nursing Posts where needed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our second thrust is to stretch your health dollar.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked about how we manage healthcare costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We keep care affordable and sustainable through a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Insurance plays a useful role in helping us stretch our resources through pooling, so that those who are ill can tap into the pool to pay for the healthcare services they need.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But insurance has an inherent risk of over-consumption.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Because through insurance, we are pooling resources and we are tapping on other people’s money in the pool to pay for our healthcare services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, we need safeguards to encourage prudence when deciding on healthcare services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam asked about Integrated Shield Plans (IPs), and I agree with Dr Tan that we can all benefit from more information-sharing and a better understanding of insurance products.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Towards this objective, MOH has facilitated several engagement sessions with insurance providers and professional bodies to foster a better understanding of the parties’ concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Dr Tan herself was present at these sessions and we benefited significantly from her contributions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have resolved some issues – not all – but discussions are still on-going.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: An important progress we have achieved is the establishment of a multilateral platform comprising Life Insurance Association, Academy of Medicine, Singapore and the Singapore Medical Association.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This platform will allow discussions to resolve issues of common concern.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are also setting up a claims management mechanism to facilitate resolution of claims-related matters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our common objective is to ensure patient care is not compromised and allow patients adequate choice, while ensuring that fees and claims remain reasonable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am confident that with this common understanding, we can find workable solutions that will benefit all parties, insurers, doctors, as well as patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked about whether IPs can be made fully portable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As IPs are commercial products, their features and pricing are ultimately determined by private insurers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But what is important is that all Singaporeans are covered under MediShield Life, regardless of their medical conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Second, we will continue to improve the healthcare system’s cost effectiveness and efficiency.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even with our best efforts, we will still be spending more on healthcare over time, given an ageing population and increasing consumption of healthcare services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We want all Singaporeans to be healthy and have access to good and affordable care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We pay particular attention to lower income households, as Mr Leon Perera highlighted, and provide them with additional support to ensure healthcare, including preventive health, remains affordable and accessible to them, and they can improve their health outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Health outcomes are influenced by multiple factors, including social, biological, cultural preferences and environmental factors, in addition to Social Economic Status, or SES.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Local studies showed that adults with lower SES do have differences in chronic disease prevalence.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: More data has been collected in the last two years including breakdown by education level as a proxy for SES, and this data will be published later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will continue to refine the data we publish.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: From local studies, we also know that adults with lower SES do have good access to care and are able to control their health conditions well.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Again, using educational attainment as a proxy for SES, among persons diagnosed with diabetes, hypertension and high blood cholesterol, over 90% of those with below Secondary school education had visited their doctor for their condition at least once in the preceding year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Further, the proportions of those with acceptable control of their medical conditions are close to the national averages.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Nonetheless, we must continue to support them to improve health outcomes and we will need to start from young, which I will talk about in a short while.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Through enhancing our healthcare financing system over the years, we have kept healthcare affordable, especially for the lower income patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our healthcare financing framework is a progressive one, overall.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Overall, government spending on healthcare has grown year after year and is likely to continue to increase.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But as Dr Tan Yia Swam mentioned, and I quote, "government subsidy is a finite thing".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That is why we have to be prudent in how we allocate limited resources, to ensure that the support we provide is more targeted to benefit those with greater need.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is our third effort – to better target subsidies, such that those with less will receive more, healthcare is kept affordable for all, and patients can be cared for at the most appropriate facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have recently enhanced the subsidies for low-income patients at the public Specialist Outpatient Clinics or SOCs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will further adjust subsidies at the SOCs by introducing two new tiers of 30% and 40% subsidy for higher income patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will enable more subsidies to be channelled to those in greater need.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With more targeted subsidies at the SOCs, we can now allow private patients discharged from our acute hospitals to choose subsidised follow-up care at the SOCs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Currently, they are treated as private patients at the SOCs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Next, we will align the means-testing basis in the acute hospitals to per capita household income which is more reflective of patients’ means, similar to the basis used for most healthcare schemes, rather than rely on personal income of the patient today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Lastly, we will also enhance subsidies at community hospitals, to keep them more affordable and facilitate the flow of patients from acute hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Taken together, these moves will ensure more targeted use of our healthcare resources, stretch our healthcare dollars, and encourage appropriate care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will go into greater detail in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In the longer term, the best way to manage healthcare costs is through our third thrust – staying healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We encourage all Singaporeans, young and old, to partner us on this journey: attend your recommended health screenings regularly, go for vaccination, and adopt healthy living habits.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I encourage all to also continue the good fight to win our on-going War on Diabetes and keep chronic conditions at bay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu will share more on this, as well as our other health promotion efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Earlier I talked about the three key thrusts, better care, stretching your dollar, and staying healthy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All our policy and measures work together to take care of the health of every Singaporean, starting from birth and throughout their life journey, keeping them as healthy as possible, for as long as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The best place to start is right at the beginning.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Minister Masagos will share our thinking on improving Child and Maternal Health, how to better support our children and their families, and to bring agencies together to co-deliver services and solutions for better outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As staying well often involves not just health but also social and other factors, we will also explore how we can pull in resources across agencies and service providers to support your overall well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng will be happy to know that they too have care coordinators to help guide their senior patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, the built environment should be designed to promote healthy living and digital tools can also be used.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: NUHS, the National University Health System, is working on this with the various agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will share more on these efforts at a later stage.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Anchoring all these transformation efforts are our healthcare staff who will continue to play a central role in our future health system, much like how they have been at the forefront line in our battle against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will elaborate on this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To conclude, as Prime Minister Lee said, it has been a year of uncertainty, anxiety, and fear.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many of us would have emerged slightly different from how we first entered.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A little more tired, more stretched, perhaps a little tougher and, I hope, a little wiser.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Partner with us as we journey forward and as we transform our healthcare system to be future-ready.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Let us work together and help all Singaporeans to stay healthy, and live well, every day of your life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, permission to take my three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, active ageing has always been an important part of successful ageing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: In the past years, HPB introduced many community programmes to encourage seniors to participate in healthy activities like group exercises and to create an avenue for neighbours to socialise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: All these have a positive impact on the resident's well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: With the COVID-19, the good work has been disrupted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Seniors are advised to stay home to reduce their exposure to the virus, as they are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But this has affected their physical and emotional well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Without the in-person group exercises and the opportunity to meet their friends, they have less motivation to exercise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But they are simply not quite the same.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Our Action Plans to encourage active ageing must evolve with the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How else can we meet the evolving needs of our future seniors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Future generations of seniors will have different lifestyle preferences and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How are we meeting the evolving needs of our seniors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: What are the measures of success and timelines for the plans?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Many seniors have benefited from the Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund (SMF).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But there is still some room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Some seniors may require a replacement device after their first device has worn out from many years of use.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Another problem is that they cannot apply for aids under the same category.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: So, if one applies for a walking stick now and gets progressively weaker over time, he might need a quad stick or walking frame but he would not be eligible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: While there are other schemes like the Assistive Technology Fund under SG Enable, the multiple schemes make things more complex than necessary for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The lack of support for the repair of devices is another handicap.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Batteries in motorised wheelchairs running out is a common problem and sometimes, these devices are perfectly usable after replacement of parts and repairs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: But SMF does not provide such support, so we have to tap on other schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: SMF also only covers consumables for applications made through a healthcare service provider like a nursing home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: If the senior is cared for at his own home, he is not eligible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I hope that the Ministry can better refine the SMF to help those in need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: The temporary suspension of certain care-giving services as well as the suspension of house visits during the circuit breaker period meant that many care-givers were on their own.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How has the plan benefited care-givers since its launch?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How can we better support care-givers, particular those who are looking after individuals with mental health conditions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Ministry look into availing more flexible homecare services to meet care-givers' needs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: There are many instances I can think of whereby care-givers need a break but they are unable to find a care institution to provide short-term care within a short notice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: For example, Mrs Koh, a resident in Yio Chu Kang, is a care-giver to her husband who has advanced dementia.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Her domestic helper is going back to her home country and there is a transition period while waiting for the new helper to arrive, given Stay-Home Notice (SHN) rules.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: As such, there needs to be more respite care options available to help care-givers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We need to give more care to our care-givers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I declare that I am a director of a social enterprise that provides care-giving services.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Care-giving is one of the most noble yet taxing responsibilities a person can take on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, many Singaporeans are called upon to become care-givers at crucial stages of their lives when their careers are developing or at a very abrupt notice when illnesses strike or accidents occur.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Be it senior loved ones, children, the infirmed or fragile, those called on to become care-givers are up to a hefty task, often having to do this on a very long-term basis and often at the expense of their careers, time with their family and, sometimes, their own mental health.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During my Budget speech, I spoke about my frazzled resident who needs 45 minutes a week to restore and refresh her spirits.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many other family care-givers I speak with also tell me that while they have made adjustments to their lives in the long-term care of their loved ones – some have resigned from their jobs, others have taken on full work-from-home arrangements, some have hired foreign domestic workers (FDWs) – the problem comes with the availability and affordability of short-term respite care.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides self-care, care-givers need short breaks from care-giving to run errands like going to the post office, picking up groceries, or even going for a much needed haircut.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To help our family care-givers balance their care-giving duties with the other responsibilities they are carrying in life, support systems like short-term respite care must be made available; and this must be affordable and accessible at very short notice.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Chairman, I was asked recently, why am I asking for a cut for MOH when they should be getting an increment for their outstanding work in this pandemic, on top of the good work that they have been doing all this while.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, a big thank you to the Minister, his team from MOH and, of course, our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Unfortunately, we have read reports of healthcare workers being abused physically and mentally while carrying out their duties.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their sacrifice and courage were met by behaviours unacceptable in any circumstances.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When the pandemic started to unfold, we hear of healthcare workers being sprayed disinfectant by neighbours, denied boarding private vehicles and many other instances on social media.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Abuse aside, we are also aware that our healthcare workers work long hours and have overnight schedules.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must provide them with the best work-life balance to maintain healthy, mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How does the Ministry plan to support our healthcare workers in this aspect?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have permission to take both cuts together?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I would also like to know the success rate at hiring people from other backgrounds into nursing – we heard some of that, I think, earlier in the debate – as well as the success rate of getting back former nurses and other women returning to work after some time off.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: On advancement, I would like to know what is being done to enhance the career paths for healthcare workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The COVID-19 pandemic showed the necessity of a whole system approach in addressing a national crisis.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Such partnerships between public and private facilities also exist outside of a crisis environment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I have had residents who are public patients telling me they were referred to Raffles Hospital for their x-rays and much to my relief at whether they were making the right decision, I learned that they were going to be offered a subsidised rate.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: As a result, they were able to get their x-rays done earlier than the queues at the public hospital would otherwise have allowed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Mr Chairman, the private hospital sector is an important part of the healthcare eco-system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: As the pandemic plays out, we may see some shifts in demand, for example, with more private sector patients opting to public care if they lose their jobs and their insurance and, of course, if there are changes to their Integrated Shield Plan (IP).

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Similarly, our private general practitioners (GPs), who play a critical role in MOH's thrust to shift healthcare beyond hospital to community as part of the goal to provide accessible, affordable and best care for all, I am heartened that we continue to build primary care capacity and strengthen primary care networks, including for mental health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But, of course, it is not just about expanding capacity, alignment of interests, incentives and processes is also key.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Having GPs and community nurses with special interests and training, giving GPs and nurses direct access to specialist advice and closer teaming and better communication with doctors, which I know some private doctors do really effectively over email and WhatsApp, giving GPs and nurses access to a broader range of diagnostic tests are proven levers to transfer care to the community and, at the same time, reducing overall demand through direct demand management at the GP level and continued education efforts to make informed patients.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Chairman, since Independence, Singapore has charted through several crises, adapted to the changing world while strengthening our social compact to keep our society strong.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many Members of this House have shared how COVID-19 has accelerated change and uncertainties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As we recover,  we must continue to renew our social compact, enabling our people to be resilient in overcoming future challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our healthcare system is a critical part of our social compact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will continue to transform it to become a proactive and inclusive care system for all Singaporeans, enabling them to attain good health and live well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will build resilience in every individual throughout life, designing our care system to address Singaporeans' health needs and risks across their life course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Today, I will highlight how we are doing this at two ends of the spectrum: first, starting well in life; and second, ageing well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For our young, we need to help them start well and achieve their fullest potential.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: International research shows that the early years of life are a critical window for development, with lasting impact on later life outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This extends to even before the child is born, during the antenatal stage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Locally, the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes, or GUSTO, found evidence that a mother's health can directly influence a child's development, which Ms Ng Ling Ling spoke about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These findings underscore the importance of intervening early in life to prevent disadvantages from snowballing, and that parents play a key role to a child's long-term development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We equip KidSTART parents with skills and knowledge to support their child's development and physical and socio-emotional well-being.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At our hospitals, the National University Hospital started an intervention programme called Promoting Parental Emotional Health to Enhance Child Learning (ProPEL).

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It supports mothers and mothers-to-be from low-income families through pregnancy into motherhood to enhance the child's development and learning.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Ms Nurdiana joined the programme during the early stages of her pregnancy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: She struggled with anxiety after being diagnosed with an auto-immune disease and had lost her job.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The ProPEL team provided psychological interventions – helping her work through her fears and anxiety on health, pregnancy and motherhood.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: With the support, Ms Nurdiana developed skills to better manage her stress and anxiety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: She is now more confident to start her journey as a mother.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The National Healthcare Group is partnering with a few Primary schools on the Living Well@School pilot.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It aims to build awareness and motivation in choosing healthier food options for the young.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Children are coached on healthier eating choices, while parents and teachers are equipped with resources to scaffold the child’s journey to embrace healthy living.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: While we have made good strides in promoting the health and well-being of children and their families upstream, we will continue to invest even more, so that we can have a healthier next generation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These are part of our larger efforts to improve the population’s health by addressing individual health needs and modifiable risk factors beyond the healthcare domain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Taskforce will focus on cross-cutting issues that require multiple agencies to collaborate and address decisively, to achieve a common goal of better health, social and education outcomes for our young.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will review our service delivery processes to integrate our services better, across the domains.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our plans will be anchored on what matters most to mothers and their children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since early this year, the Taskforce has already started engaging various groups of parents and stakeholders, to better understand their challenges in fostering a healthy lifestyle in their children and in accessing services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We found their feedback very insightful and will continue to facilitate more conversations throughout the year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Next, on the second group – our seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: While COVID-19 has posed many challenges, it also presents us with new opportunities to further transform our support for them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since its launch in 2015, we have made significant progress on many fronts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have raised the retirement age, provided seniors with opportunities to learn and volunteer, and rolled out the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Nevertheless, our plans must continue to evolve to meet the needs and aspirations of current and future generations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Achieving these aspirations is only possible through a whole-of-society, citizen-centric effort that brings together everyone to “turn silver into gold”.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In my previous job, I was turning "waste into wealth"; this time, I am trying to turn "silver into gold".

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am glad to share with Mr Yip Hon Weng that we have started engagement sessions since last October to partner citizens on the Refreshed Action Plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I encourage everyone to join this meaningful national SGTogether effort!

speaker: The Second Minister for Health (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Having participated in some sessions myself, I am deeply encouraged by the diverse discussions and participants’ aspirations to age well.
