text: Thirty-seven point five percent of Malays and 36.1% of Chinese have higher blood pressure, compared to 29.5% for Indians.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For cancers, the Chinese consistently have the highest age-standardised cancer incidence rates, but the proportion of Malays among all cases of cancer has gradually increased over the decades.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Looking upstream at other modifiable lifestyle risk factors, the Malays have the highest obesity rates and Indians have the highest prevalence of being overweight.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The prevalence of daily smokers are more than twice as high amongst the Malays as compared to the Chinese and Indians.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Research has shown, poor health behaviours can affect life expectancy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Therefore, our community needs to take stronger action, and support one another against poor health habits.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Cultural preferences may influence health behaviours and we recognise the importance of engagement and collaboration with the different ethnic minority groups to design culturally relevant programmes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some of our earlier efforts have seen good progress.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For the Malay community, we have built our partnerships under HPB's Jaga Kesihatan, Jaga Ummah from 23 in 2018 to 32 mosque partners, and 18 other partners such as the Malay Executive Activity Committees (MAEC) and MENDAKI.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With their support, we were able to provide a range of healthy living programmes for their congregants.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our Indian community partners such as Hindu Endowment Board, Sikh Welfare Council, SINDA and places of worship have provided strong support in engagement efforts with their networks.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, NARPANI Pearavai provides Indian Activity Executive Committees funding to co-create health activities for their residents.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will build on early successes to improve our work, to make healthy living a sustainable achievement.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Moving forward, we will expand community partnerships and harness ground-up efforts to multiply our impact and and ensure that our programmes are culturally relevant through customisation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will engage key community leaders through significant platforms to garner commitment towards health.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, at a forum in end-March 2021, leaders from the Hindu Endowment Board, SINDA, NARPANI, Sikh Welfare Council and HPB will discuss the state of health amongst Indians and co-develop culturally relevant efforts to facilitate healthier lifestyles among Singaporean Indians.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We look forward to an invigorating discussion and a year of fun, healthier activities for all Singapore Indian residents.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to say a few words in Malay, please.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue to collaborate with the "Jaga Kesihatan, Jaga Ummah" (JKJU) network and community leaders to develop and implement health programmes throughout the year to foster good health habits.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will produce simple tips to remind the Malay community about the important steps to take care of their health.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To sustain this effort on health, we will have Health Ambassadors and continue to enlarge this network of volunteers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As a member of the Macpherson MAEC, she plans motivational health lectures for the Malay community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She also spends time teaching our seniors to surf the Internet.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In English): Beyond ethnic minorities, I echo what Minister Masagos said on the importance of supporting our children and women to lead healthy lives for a healthier next generation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is key to support couples who wish to start their own families.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about supporting couples undergoing IVF.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, eligible Singaporean couples undergoing Assisted Conception Procedures, or ACP, in public Assisted Reproduction centres can receive co-funding support for the different procedures.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As such, there is no remaining balance to be rolled over.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, MOH regularly reviews the clinical evidence around the number of cycles to co-fund.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: At present, on average, women undergo two ART cycles before achieving pregnancy successfully.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Evidence shows that the success rate of ART decreases with maternal age, as each successful cycle progresses.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is not just about Government funding, but the strain of couples to keep trying.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Hence, we must continue to encourage couples to marry and start families early, to maximise the chances of conception.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: After co-funding, the current MediSave per-cycle limits are generally sufficient to cover the cost of a ACP cycle at public Assisted Reproduction Centres.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As not all couples go through multiple cycles, we have allowed a higher MediSave withdrawal limit for the first two cycles so that more of the lifetime limit can be used.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MediSave can be used to pay for all standard procedures for each method of treatment, such as the priming of the uterus, egg recovery and fertilisation processes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, as Traditional Chinese Medicine treatments associated with IVF are not part of mainstream evidence-based treatment, there are no plans to allow MediSave for their use currently.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MOH remains committed towards supporting Singaporean couples in their parenting journeys, and will continue to review the MediSave withdrawal limits to ensure they remain relevant and adequate for Singaporeans, as we balance immediate expenses with retaining sufficient savings for basic healthcare needs in old age.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Apart from supporting couples, we enabled early intervention and enhanced subsidies for vaccinations under the National Childhood Immunisation Schedule, or NCIS, for all Singaporean children at polyclinics, and extended them to CHAS GP clinics across Singapore in November 2020.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have also added vaccines against chicken pox, influenza and pneumococcal disease to the NCIS.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For Singaporean children up to the age of six, we have extended full subsidies for childhood developmental screenings at CHAS GP clinics, to allow for early detection and timely intervention for any developmental delays.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: From last November, subsidies have been extended to vaccinations under the National Adult Immunisation Schedule, or NAIS, at CHAS GP clinics and polyclinics for all eligible Singaporean adults.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about the progress of our national immunisation efforts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One of the families that benefited is the Chiam family.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The three-generational family has been regularly consulting Dr Lim Hong Shen from A Medical Clinic, under the NUHS Primary Care Network.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With Dr Lim's strong support, their two children, aged two and four years old, have undergone their childhood developmental screenings and received subsidised vaccinations for influenza, as well as measles, mumps and rubella.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The grandfather, aged 69 years old, has also received both the pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We hope that this improved accessibility and affordability will encourage Singaporeans to protect themselves and their families against vaccine-preventable diseases by getting vaccinated as recommended, and support children in starting off well and healthy.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MOH is committed to increase the uptake of nationally recommended vaccinations, and will encourage eligible Singaporeans to be vaccinated.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Together, we can encourage one another to take greater ownership of our health and lead healthier lives, for a better future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: By way of clarifications, I have one observation and one question.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: First, regarding the Senior Minister of State, Dr Janil's observation that relooking healthcare needs to be through the lens of longer term issues in a COVID-19 world and looking at the larger social eco-system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: It is essential in our approach to society and healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I have a follow-up question for the Senior Minister of State, Dr Koh, regarding the earlier point in my speech on the approach to outsourcing hospital cleaners and hospital attendants.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I do not expect an immediate resolution to this question, but I will urge a longer term rethink once the COVID-19 crisis is over.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: After all, COVID-19 has raised many questions of countries around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: If it is supply chains, countries are looking, "at just in time" as compared to "just in case".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And may I suggest that on issues of workforce, we also may want to look at economies of efficiency, but juxtaposing this and considering as well the resilience of solidarity across the entire healthcare team.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And I hope MOH will consider this as part of a longer term review for the COVID-19 world, and what comes next.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because if they are a small number, for which there is little career progression, we need to also bear that in mind to balance out the needs of the organisation versus the aspirations of the person.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Regarding the vaccination programme, I am happy to hear that a huge percentage of our seniors has been vaccinated for flu as well as for pneumococcal.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The issue now is, of course, the outreach to the rest.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There is currently now no specific outreach programme to reach out to seniors that have not been vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: So, I hope that MOH can review this and then take a look.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When I take a look at the HealthHub apps, there is immunisation charge based on age, but the age stops at 26 years old.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: So, can MOH take a look at it to see how to expand that further.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: My second clarification goes to the Senior Minister of State Janil.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Looking back, do we have the ability to do so?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are, indeed, still developing the platform and we will be adding more information.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, I will bring this back and then we will develop it further.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The key thing about vaccination is getting them to be aware of it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, we did try to roll out a public education campaign and this is something that we can build on.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The other thing is to work with the General Practitioners (GPs), with the doctors, to get them to routinely advise their patients on vaccination needs, especially every time they come to visit, we would ask them to inform their patients, so that this will also increase awareness and their interest and uptake for vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I understand the Member's questions correctly, if an outbreak had occurred now?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: With the capability we had then or the capability we have now?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, with the capability that we had in October 2019, would we have picked up COVID-19 outbreak in October 2019?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We pick up outbreaks of disease on a regular basis.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our level of paranoia, anxiety, concern about this increased after SARS, as a result of which clinical teams across the healthcare network have to report any number of either confirmed or suspected infectious diseases.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the real answer is not really whether we would have picked it up, but how quickly would we have picked it up and how quickly would we have responded and put in place many of these strategies that we now see as normal for containing disease outbreak.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Whether it is the testing, the tracing, speed of that, the ability to quarantine individuals, the ability to do the sequencing and stand up therapeutics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, certainly, our capabilities have improved and increased quite significantly since the first outbreak.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the short answer to the Member's question is yes but we can do it much better today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One of the reasons why we can do it much better today is because this is not SARS.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have learned the lessons from SARS, we have learned the lessons from COVID-19, and we have to prepare that Disease X, the next pandemic and the next crisis, will be like neither.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And we need that institutional agility and institutional capability to deal with the unknown, which is one of the more difficult things that we have to do.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is I think the Ministers and the Senior Ministers of State did not answer my query on how the public health services are being priced, whether it is based on marginal cost or average cost.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Maybe I add a bit more information on that, specifically about whether it is based on amortisation of assets, land cost, rental cost, all these – I hope to be clarified.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second question is on MediShield Life insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am actually still very puzzled why our healthcare insurance schemes are left open-ended.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because as one gets older, as Singaporeans get older, they will find it more and more unaffordable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have also spoken in my speech that when Singaporeans get older like 80 years old or 90 years old, the premium will become very high.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, under two scenarios, when you keep the premium —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leong, can we not have a speech?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Just ask your clarifications borne out of the responses of the Political Office Holders (POHs).

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, please get to the point of your clarification.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, those are the questions I would like further clarification on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because these are very important; has to be answered.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, I will attempt to explain the MediShield Life premium issue.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I do not think he understood what was said in the House last year and I urge him to read my speech all over again in Hansard.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But my question really is whether MOH has a view or is it currently embarking on any kind of study or upstream prevention campaigns, in the likes of when we identified diabetes to be a big healthcare crisis for Singapore, then we went on a very national campaign and we looked into reducing sugar and salt in our food in the hawker centre and so on.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I remember when I was a child in Primary School, I was also in the Trim and Fit (TAF) Club to address obesity.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tan, if you could kindly ask your clarification.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: My question is: does MOH have a view or intention to study how we can embark on a prevention strategy to avoid this continuing trend of high incidence of mental health or mental illness amongst our population in the long run?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not just MOH that is interested in this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is an area where the academics and the professionals working with people with mental health issues are very interested in looking at.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is not going to be an area that we can have complete prevention.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We also have to research into areas about how we can help people cope and mitigate the mental health issues that they come across.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not going to be easy to pinpoint a single factor, just like diabetes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While we can concentrate our efforts on sugar or weight loss activity, we will have a variety of things to direct attention and the efforts of the individual in the family.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the reality is it is a wide space with many different causes and many different paths through it, and it will be something that requires effort from a multi-disciplinary team and, indeed, the whole of society.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the short answer is yes, we are very interested in this.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister, my apologies, I did not see your hand.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And, very often, is not just a medical issue.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, it is a multi-pronged approach and it requires a whole-of-society involvement in this, particularly in preventive mental health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Because it requires a lot of support in the community to work with us, work with various Ministries and agencies, so that, together, we can better address the challenges of mental well-being and help our Singaporeans, particularly, the young, to be better prepared for the challenges that they are going to see, so that we can strengthen their resilience against mental challenges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: First, can I confirm the Ministry's definition of PCHI is based on family members living under the same roof?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Second, what is the Ministry's main concern about allowing greater use of MediSave in polyclinics, SOCs and restructured hospitals?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I know MOH is worried about premature depletion of the MediSave accounts.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, MediSave can only be used for medically necessary treatments, and the risk of doctors in these public institutions over-treating is minimal.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And patients there also have little discretion to demand unnecessary treatment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: On the flip side, patients do retain their discretion to skip treatment to reduce out-of-pocket payments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This will impact the success of their treatment that may cause both the patient and the Government more in the long term.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can MOH reconsider how prudent it still is to restrict the use of MediSave in these public healthcare institutions?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Member for asking the clarifications.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In terms of liberalising MediSave usage, we have through the years, allowed more and more uses for MediSave.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: You will remember that when we first started with the Chronic Disease Management (CDMP), there were only a few conditions that were in it.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are always opening further opportunity to use MediSave, and as the Member pointed out, they could well be situations in which we could liberalise some more and we will continue to do so.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have got time for just two more clarifications, so could I invite Members to keep them short?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I am glad to hear from Minister Masagoes that the Ministry is reviewing the Senior Mobility and Enabling Fund.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Can the Ministry provide more details about the focus area of review and when will the review be completed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There is quite a fair bit of good suggestions out there on IVF and that is why I filed so many cuts, Parliamentary Questions and Adjournment Motion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Could I ask whether MOH can consider setting up a citizen workgroup to really deep dive into this issue of IVF here in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am sure that this is something we can consider and I will follow up with the Member after the Budget and Committee of Supply debates are over.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My clarification on the pricing of the public health services has not been answered.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am afraid Mr Leong, it is 5.50 pm, which is the guillotine time for this Head.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, Dr Tan Wu Meng, if would like to withdraw your amendment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Perhaps I can just give a very quick answer.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, we take into account all the costs that healthcare institutions incurred, because someone has to pay for these costs – whether it is the Government, whether it is the patient, whether it is the institution.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Having costed them fully, the Government then provides subvention to cover the bulk of the cost of operation and the cost of investment in the building of the infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On top of that, we provide subvention for the patients when they go and see the doctors or they receive treatment at these healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: So, yes, we account for the cost of the building and the delivery of services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But at the same time, we provide subvention and subsidies for the patients and for the institutions' operations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Mr Chairman, I thank all Members for their cuts and I thank our Ministers, Senior Ministers of State, Parliamentary Secretary at MOH for their responses and sharing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: It does not rest and so are our healthcare frontliners, our agencies, our MOH officials have also had many sleepless nights because of this COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Presumably, with implications for sleep health as Parliamentary Secretary shared earlier.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: So, a big thank you to all who keep us safe, and in doing so, keep Singapore going.
